big: The RBI has just cut the repo rate. The headline says rates are falling, and a client wants to rush into a long-term debt fund. But a bond fund is priced off a whole curve, not a single rate.

lines: RBI cut rates. Should I buy a long-term debt fund?
Maybe. But which rates fell: the short ones or the long ones? Let us draw the curve and watch what a cut moves.

alt: A line of yields rising with the years to maturity
caps: A yield curve plots the yield of bonds against their maturity. Here a 3-month bond yields 6.5%.
Longer bonds pay more. At 10 years the yield is 7.3%, which is 0.8 points above the 3-month rate.
An upward slope is a normal curve: you are paid to lend for longer. These yields are made up.

rows: Years of extra yield to repay it
alt: Steep curve versus flat curve: extra yield for lending ten years instead of one against the price fall if yields rise
caps: Steep curve: a 10-year bond yields 1.8 points more than a 1-year bond. Flat curve: just 0.2 points.
Either way, a 10-year bond has a duration of about 7, so a 1% rise in yields cuts its price about 7%.
Steep: about 3.9 years of extra yield repays that fall. Flat: about 35 years.
A steep curve rewards extending maturity. A flat or inverted curve does not.

alt: The yield curve moving after a repo rate cut
caps: Before the cut: 3-month yield 6.5%, 10-year yield 7.3%. Then the repo rate is cut by 0.50%.
The curve is drawn. Now the cut arrives.
The short end follows the repo rate straight away: the 3-month yield falls to 6.0%.
The 10-year yield stays near 7.3%. A long-duration fund gains little from this cut.

q: The RBI cuts the repo rate by 0.50%. The 3-month yield falls from 6.5% to 6.0%, but the 10-year stays at 7.3%. A client wants a long-duration fund because rates are falling. What is the fair reply?
opts: Do it now, since a repo cut always lowers every yield on the curve
The long end moves first, so a long fund will gain before short ones do
Avoid all debt funds for a year until the new repo rate settles in
The cut moved the short end only, so a long fund gains little from it alone
why: The repo rate mainly anchors the short end. The long end follows growth, inflation and bond supply, so it may not follow.
The short end responds first, as it tracks the repo rate. The long end responds to other things, and here it did not.
Waiting a year is not a plan. Short-duration funds could benefit from the lower short-end yields right away.
The long end did not fall, so long bond prices did not rise. Her gain would depend on a later fall in long yields.

q: The curve is inverted: the 1-year yield is 7.4% and the 10-year yield is 6.8%. A client wants a home for money she needs in one year. Which reading is sound?
opts: Long bonds pay less here, so a short fund earns more with less rate risk
Go long, since the 10-year bond has the biggest price upside in a rate cut
Wait, since inverted curves mean every debt fund will fall next month
Pick the 10-year bond, as it pays 6.8% for ten years of safety
why: Short yields exceed long ones, so there is no reward for taking duration. A short fund yields more and swings less.
The 10-year pays less than the 1-year, and its price would swing much more. She needs the money in a year anyway.
An inverted curve does not predict a debt fund fall next month. It only shows that short yields are above long ones.
A 10-year bond is not 'safer' for ten years. It carries more price risk than a 1-year bond, and she needs her money in one.

q: On a steep curve, a 10-year bond yields 1.8 points more than a 1-year bond and has a duration of about 7. If yields rise 1% at once, about how long does the extra yield take to repay the price fall?
opts: About 7 years, since the repayment time equals the duration
About 0.3 years, since 1.8 is much bigger than 1
About 3.9 years, which is 7% divided by 1.8% a year
It never repays, because a price fall is permanent
why: The repayment time is the fall divided by the extra yield, not simply the duration. Here that gives 3.9, not 7.
1.8% extra a year is not enough to cover a 7% fall in under a year. Dividing 1 by 1.8 is not the right sum here.
A price fall of about 7% against 1.8% extra a year takes 3.9 years of extra yield to make up.
A price fall can be made up by extra income, and the bond is pulled back to face value as it nears maturity.

q: A client with a goal in two years wants a long-duration fund because a rate cut is expected. Which advice fits what the lesson says about duration?
opts: Go all in, since a cut is expected and the fund can wait out any dip
Skip debt completely, because rate cuts only help equity funds
Choose the longest fund, because longer maturity always pays more
Treat duration as a rate bet: size it small, match her horizon
why: An expected cut is not a delivered one. If yields do not fall, a long fund can dip within her two-year window.
Rate cuts can help bond prices as well as equities. The issue is sizing duration, not avoiding debt.
Longer maturity pays more only on a normal curve, and only if rates behave. It also raises risk.
Duration is a view on the path of rates, so keep it small, and check that the horizon is not shorter than the duration.

pts: A normal curve slopes upward. Flat pays little extra to lend longer. Inverted means short yields exceed long ones.
The repo rate mostly anchors the short end. The long end follows growth, inflation and bond supply.
Long duration is a view on the path of rates. Size it carefully.
